newsitem.title: GERMANY: German jobs not going abroad yet- RWI institute.
newsitem.headline: German jobs not going abroad yet- RWI institute.

text.p: A leading think-tank on Monday contested the widespread view that Germany's hard mark currency and high labour costs were driving jobs abroad and keeping unemployment at home near post-war highs.
The Essen-based RWI institute said in a report that, based on a five-year survey of 80 big firms, those that took on new workers abroad also hired staff in Germany.
"In other words -- companies that strongly increased worker numbers abroad also expanded their staff at home," the report said. "There is no evidence of job migration."
But the institute warned that the rapid globalisation of the German economy did pose a long-term threat to jobs at home.
"There is little evidence yet that the globalisation of the German economy would have a negative impact on domestic jobs. But this is only the case in the short term," the report said.

"In the long term the number of options with which companies can react to fluctuations in demand and pressures to cut costs will increase -- and with every direct investment their room for maneouvre will expand."
The RWI report comes as Germany battles with unemployment of close to four million which is refusing to shrink despite a modest economic recovery.

Bonn has just defused a row with the European Union over subsidies for two new Volkswagen AG car plants in the eastern state of Saxony which would create 23,000 new jobs. VW had threatened to take its investment to eastern Europe if it did not get the state aid.

RWI, one of the six top German economic institutes, said that the proportion of workers employed abroad by the companies had risen from 31 percent in 1990 to over 36 percent in 1995 -- apparently indicating that jobs were moving abroad.

But, the RWI said, a closer look revealed that there was a positive correlation between companies hiring staff abroad and taking on extra workers at home in the years 1990-94. There was, however, a rising trend in the total share of workers being taken on abroad, from half in 1990 to 80 percent in 1995.
Mergers and acquisitions -- investments where opportunities to relocate jobs quickly are limited -- were the main form of expansion from 1990-92, the RWI said.
But the number of new ventures, where job substitution is easier, climbed to over half by 1995. Many were in low-cost countries like China and other developing Asian states.
